stem: The velocity-time graph of a particle moving along a straight line is shown. In the time interval 0 to 40 s, the velocity increases linearly from 0 to +20 m/s in 10 s, stays constant at 20 m/s for 10 s (to t=20s), decreases linearly to 0 at t=30s, and reaches -20 m/s at t=40s. Find the total distance travelled and the average velocity during this 40 s period.
raw_stem: The velocity-time graph of a particle moving along a straight line is shown. In the time interval 0 to 40 s, the velocity increases linearly from 0 to +20 m/s in 10 s, stays constant at 20 m/s for 10 s (to t=20s), decreases linearly to 0 at t=30s, and reaches -20 m/s at t=40s. Find the total distance travelled and the average velocity during this 40 s period.
subject: Physics
formula: Distance S = ∫|v|dt,  Displacement Δx = ∫v dt,  v_avg = Δx / Δt
steps: Split the v-t graph wherever the velocity law changes and at the sign change.
0–10 s: triangle area = ½(10)(20) = +100 m.
10–20 s: rectangle area = (10)(20) = +200 m.
20–30 s: triangle area = ½(10)(20) = +100 m.
30–40 s: triangle lies below the time axis, so signed area = -½(10)(20) = -100 m.
Total distance = 100 + 200 + 100 + 100 = 500 m.
Net displacement = 100 + 200 + 100 - 100 = +300 m.
Average velocity = displacement / total time = 300/40 = +7.5 m/s.
trap: Distance is the scalar path length ∫|v|dt; never subtract the negative area when calculating distance!
teacher_check: Recompute signed area and absolute area separately; the two agree only when v never changes sign.

stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with position x(t) = 6t - t² (in meters). What is the total distance travelled by the particle between t = 0 and t = 5 s?
raw_stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with position x(t) = 6t - t² (in meters). What is the total distance travelled by the particle between t = 0 and t = 5 s?
subject: Physics
formula: v(t) = dx/dt = 0 ⇒ t_turn; S = |x(t_turn) - x(0)| + |x(5) - x(t_turn)|
steps: Differentiate position: v(t) = dx/dt = 6 - 2t.
Identify turning point where v = 0: 6 - 2t = 0 ⇒ t_turn = 3 s.
Evaluate position at key moments: x(0) = 0 m; x(3) = 6(3) - 3² = 18 - 9 = 9 m; x(5) = 6(5) - 5² = 30 - 25 = 5 m.
Distance in forward segment (0 to 3 s): S₁ = |x(3) - x(0)| = |9 - 0| = 9 m.
Distance in reverse segment (3 to 5 s): S₂ = |x(5) - x(3)| = |5 - 9| = 4 m.
Total distance travelled S = S₁ + S₂ = 9 + 4 = 13 m.
Net displacement is merely x(5) - x(0) = 5 m!
trap: Plugging t = 5 directly into x(t) yields displacement (5 m), completely ignoring the 4 m retraced backward!
teacher_check: Differentiate x(t): v=6-2t. At t=3 s, v=0 and x=9 m; x(5)=5 m, so distance is 9+4=13 m.

stem: The position of a particle is given by x(t) = 4t³ - 18t² + 24t + 2 (in meters). Find the acceleration of the particle at the instant when its instantaneous velocity is zero for the second time.
raw_stem: The position of a particle is given by x(t) = 4t³ - 18t² + 24t + 2 (in meters). Find the acceleration of the particle at the instant when its instantaneous velocity is zero for the second time.
subject: Physics
steps: Velocity v(t) = dx/dt = 12t² - 36t + 24.
The roots are t₁ = 1 s and t₂ = 2 s.
The second turning point occurs at t = 2 s.
Acceleration function a(t) = dv/dt = 24t - 36.
trap: Never assume acceleration is zero at a turning point! At t = 2 s, v = 0 but acceleration is +12 m/s².
teacher_check: Differentiate twice and verify at the second zero of v: v=12(t-1)(t-2), a=24t-36, so a(2)=12 m/s².

stem: A body travels the first half of a total distance D with speed v₁ = 30 km/h and the remaining half with speed v₂ = 60 km/h. Its average speed over the total journey is:
raw_stem: A body travels the first half of a total distance D with speed v₁ = 30 km/h and the remaining half with speed v₂ = 60 km/h. Its average speed over the total journey is:
subject: Physics
formula: v_avg = Total Distance / Total Time = 2 v₁ v₂ / (v₁ + v₂)
steps: Time for first half: t₁ = (D/2) / v₁ = D / (2v₁).
Time for second half: t₂ = (D/2) / v₂ = D / (2v₂).
Total time: T = t₁ + t₂ = (D/2) (1/v₁ + 1/v₂) = (D/2) ((v₁ + v₂) / (v₁ v₂)).
Average speed: v_avg = D / T = 2 v₁ v₂ / (v₁ + v₂) (Harmonic Mean).
Substitute values: v_avg = 2(30)(60) / (30 + 60) = 3600 / 90 = 40 km/h.
trap: Average speed for equal distances is the HARMONIC mean, NOT the arithmetic mean (30+60)/2 = 45 km/h!
teacher_check: Use equal half-distances: total time is D/(2v1)+D/(2v2), giving the harmonic mean 2v1v2/(v1+v2).

stem: A particle moves in a straight line such that its displacement x at time t is related by t = α x² + β x, where α and β are positive constants. The acceleration of the particle in terms of velocity v is:
raw_stem: A particle moves in a straight line such that its displacement x at time t is related by t = α x² + β x, where α and β are positive constants. The acceleration of the particle in terms of velocity v is:
subject: Physics
formula: dt/dx = 1/v = 2αx + β;  d/dx(1/v) = -v⁻² dv/dx;  a = v dv/dx
steps: Differentiate t with respect to x: dt/dx = 2αx + β.
Since v = dx/dt, we have 1/v = 2αx + β.
Differentiate both sides with respect to x: -1/v² · (dv/dx) = 2α.
Multiply both sides by -v²: dv/dx = -2α v².
Acceleration a = v (dv/dx) = v (-2α v²) = -2α v³.
trap: Chain rule execution: differentiating with respect to x gives dv/dx, then multiplying by v gives a = v(dv/dx) = -2α v³.
teacher_check: From 1/v=2αx+β, differentiate with respect to x: dv/dx=-2αv², then a=v dv/dx=-2αv³.

stem: The velocity-displacement (v-x) graph of a particle moving in a straight line is a straight line with negative slope: v(x) = -m x + v₀ (where m, v₀ > 0). The corresponding acceleration-displacement (a-x) graph is:
raw_stem: The velocity-displacement (v-x) graph of a particle moving in a straight line is a straight line with negative slope: v(x) = -m x + v₀ (where m, v₀ > 0). The corresponding acceleration-displacement (a-x) graph is:
subject: Physics
formula: a = v (dv/dx) = (-mx + v₀)(-m) = m² x - m v₀
steps: Given: v = -mx + v₀.
Slope of v-x graph: dv/dx = -m (constant negative slope).
Fundamental relation: a = v (dv/dx).
Substitute: a(x) = (-mx + v₀) · (-m) = m² x - m v₀.
Compare with standard line equation y = M x + C:
Slope M = m² > 0 (strictly positive slope!).
y-intercept C = -m v₀ < 0 (negative intercept).
Hence, the a-x plot is a straight line with POSITIVE slope!
trap: Negative v-x slope produces a POSITIVE a-x slope because (-m) × (-m) = +m²!
teacher_check: Differentiate the loaded v(x): dv/dx=-1.5; multiplying by v(x) gives an a-x line with slope +(1.5)².

stem: The v² versus x graph of a particle moving in a straight line is a straight line passing through (0, 100) and (25, 0) (where v is in m/s and x is in m). The magnitude of acceleration of the particle is:
raw_stem: The v² versus x graph of a particle moving in a straight line is a straight line passing through (0, 100) and (25, 0) (where v is in m/s and x is in m). The magnitude of acceleration of the particle is:
subject: Physics
formula: v² = u² + 2ax ⇒ Slope of v²-x graph = 2a ⇒ a = ½ (Slope)
steps: From the 3rd equation of kinematics: v² = u² + 2ax.
This is of the linear form Y = M X + C, where Y = v², X = x, C = u², and Slope M = 2a.
Calculate slope from given points: M = (0 - 100) / (25 - 0) = -100 / 25 = -4 m/s².
Since Slope = 2a, we have 2a = -4 ⇒ a = -2 m/s².
The magnitude of acceleration is |a| = 2 m/s².
trap: Forgetting the factor of 2: the slope of v²-x is 2a, NOT a!
teacher_check: The v²-x slope is -4, so 2a=-4 and a=-2 m/s²; magnitude is 2 m/s².

stem: The acceleration-time (a-t) graph of a particle starting from rest at t = 0 is a triangle with base from t = 0 to t = 8 s and peak acceleration a_max = 6 m/s² at t = 4 s. The maximum velocity reached by the particle is:
raw_stem: The acceleration-time (a-t) graph of a particle starting from rest at t = 0 is a triangle with base from t = 0 to t = 8 s and peak acceleration a_max = 6 m/s² at t = 4 s. The maximum velocity reached by the particle is:
subject: Physics
formula: Δv = v_final - v_initial = Area under a-t graph
steps: Initial velocity v(0) = 0 (starts from rest).
Change in velocity Δv = ∫ a dt = Area under a-t graph.
The graph is a single positive triangle with base b = 8 s and height h = 6 m/s².
Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 8 × 6 = 24 m/s.
Since a ≥ 0 throughout, velocity increases monotonically and reaches its maximum at t = 8 s.
trap: Do not stop integration at peak acceleration (t = 4 s); acceleration remains positive until t = 8 s, so velocity keeps rising!
teacher_check: Velocity change is the signed area under the a-t graph: ½(8)(6)=24 m/s.

stem: A particle moves such that its acceleration a versus displacement x is given by a(x) = 3x² + 2x. If the particle starts from origin (x = 0) with initial velocity v = 2 m/s, its velocity when it reaches x = 2 m is:
raw_stem: A particle moves such that its acceleration a versus displacement x is given by a(x) = 3x² + 2x. If the particle starts from origin (x = 0) with initial velocity v = 2 m/s, its velocity when it reaches x = 2 m is:
subject: Physics
formula: ∫ v dv = ∫ a(x) dx ⇒ ½(v² - u²) = Area under a-x curve
steps: Use differential work-energy relation: a = v (dv/dx) ⇒ v dv = a(x) dx.
Integrate both sides from x = 0 (v = 2) to x = 2 (v = v_f):
∫₂^{v_f} v dv = ∫₀² (3x² + 2x) dx.
LHS: ½ (v_f² - 2²) = ½ (v_f² - 4).
Equate: ½ (v_f² - 4) = 12 ⇒ v_f² - 4 = 24 ⇒ v_f² = 28.
trap: Area under a-x curve equals CHANGE IN KINETIC ENERGY PER UNIT MASS, ½(v² - u²), NOT simply v - u!
teacher_check: Integrate v dv=a(x)dx: ½(v²-4)=∫₀²(3x²+2x)dx=12, hence v²=28.

stem: A gas balloon is going up with a constant velocity of 10 m/s. When this balloon reached a height of 75 m from the ground, a stone is dropped from it while the balloon continues rising with the same velocity. The height of the balloon when the stone hits the ground is: (Take g = 10 m/s²)
raw_stem: A gas balloon is going up with a constant velocity of 10 m/s. When this balloon reached a height of 75 m from the ground, a stone is dropped from it while the balloon continues rising with the same velocity. The height of the balloon when the stone hits the ground is: (Take g = 10 m/s²)
subject: Physics
formula: y_stone(t) = h + u t - ½ g t² = 0;  h_balloon(t) = h + u t
steps: CRITICAL INHERITANCE: The dropped stone inherits the balloon's upward velocity: u_stone = +10 m/s.
Equation of vertical motion for stone with origin at ground (upwards positive):
When stone hits ground, y(t) = 0: 5 t² - 10 t - 75 = 0 ⇒ t² - 2 t - 15 = 0.
Factor quadratic: (t - 5)(t + 3) = 0 ⇒ t = 5 s (since t > 0).
During these 5 s, the balloon continues rising at steady 10 m/s:
Height of balloon at t = 5 s: H = 75 + (10 m/s × 5 s) = 75 + 50 = 125 m.
trap: Assuming dropped stone has u = 0 leads to t = √(2h/g) = √15 ≈ 3.87 s and completely incorrect balloon height!
teacher_check: Substitute t=5 s into both trajectories: the stone reaches y=0 while the balloon reaches 125 m.

stem: Water drops fall from a tap on the floor 5 m below at regular time intervals. The first drop strikes the floor at the exact instant the sixth drop begins to fall. The height of the fourth drop from the ground at that instant is: (Take g = 10 m/s²)
raw_stem: Water drops fall from a tap on the floor 5 m below at regular time intervals. The first drop strikes the floor at the exact instant the sixth drop begins to fall. The height of the fourth drop from the ground at that instant is: (Take g = 10 m/s²)
subject: Physics
formula: s_n = ½ g (n Δt)²;  H_total = ½ g (N-1)² Δt²
steps: Let the regular time interval between successive drops be Δt.
When the 6th drop begins to fall, the 1st drop has already fallen for 5 intervals: T = 5Δt.
For the 1st drop, 5 = ½(10)(5Δt)² = 125Δt², so Δt² = 0.04 and Δt = 0.20 s.
At the same instant, the 4th drop has been falling for 2 intervals: t₄ = 2Δt = 0.40 s.
Distance fallen by the 4th drop = ½(10)(0.40)² = 0.80 m.
Height of the 4th drop above the floor = 5.00 - 0.80 = 4.20 m.
trap: Careful with drop indexing! The 4th drop has experienced 2 intervals of fall, NOT 4 intervals. Also remember question asks for height FROM GROUND, not distance from tap!
teacher_check: Check the clock indexing: first drop has 5 intervals, fourth has 2; Δt=0.2 s and the fourth is 4.2 m above the floor.

stem: A paratrooper after bailing out falls 50 m without friction. When the parachute opens, he decelerates downwards at 2 m/s². He reaches the ground with a speed of 3 m/s. At what height did he bail out? (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
raw_stem: A paratrooper after bailing out falls 50 m without friction. When the parachute opens, he decelerates downwards at 2 m/s². He reaches the ground with a speed of 3 m/s. At what height did he bail out? (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
subject: Physics
formula: v₁² = 2 g h₁;  v₂² = v₁² - 2 a_brake h₂;  H = h₁ + h₂
steps: Phase 1 (Free Fall): h₁ = 50 m, initial speed u = 0, acceleration g = 9.8 m/s².
Velocity when chute opens: v₁² = u² + 2 g h₁ = 0 + 2(9.8)(50) = 980 (m/s)².
Phase 2 (Decelerated Descent): Initial velocity v₁, landing velocity v₂ = 3 m/s, deceleration a = 2 m/s².
Apply 3rd equation: v₂² = v₁² - 2 a h₂ ⇒ 3² = 980 - 2(2) h₂.
Total bail-out height H = h₁ + h₂ = 50 + 242.75 = 292.75 m ≈ 293 m.
trap: The terminal speed of Phase 1 is the INITIAL speed of Phase 2. Piecewise boundary matching is mandatory!
teacher_check: State continuity check: v1²=2gh1=980; the same v1 enters phase 2, giving h2=242.75 m and H=292.75 m.

stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from the top of a tower of height h with velocity u. It reaches the ground in time t₁. If it is thrown vertically downwards from the same spot with the same speed u, it reaches the ground in time t₂. If it is simply dropped from rest, the time t₃ taken to reach the ground is:
raw_stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from the top of a tower of height h with velocity u. It reaches the ground in time t₁. If it is thrown vertically downwards from the same spot with the same speed u, it reaches the ground in time t₂. If it is simply dropped from rest, the time t₃ taken to reach the ground is:
subject: Physics
formula: -h = u t₁ - ½ g t₁²;  -h = -u t₂ - ½ g t₂²;  h = ½ g t₃²
steps: Case 1 (Thrown Up): -h = u t₁ - ½ g t₁² ⇒ ½ g t₁² - u t₁ - h = 0.
Case 2 (Thrown Down): -h = -u t₂ - ½ g t₂² ⇒ ½ g t₂² + u t₂ - h = 0.
Eliminating u between the two quadratic roots yields: h = ½ g (t₁ t₂).
For free drop from rest: h = ½ g t₃².
Equating gives t₃² = t₁ t₂ ⇒ t₃ = √(t₁ t₂).
trap: This beautiful invariant shows the geometric mean relationship: t₃ is neither the arithmetic mean nor root-mean-square!
teacher_check: Eliminate u between the upward/downward equations to obtain h=½gt1t2; compare with h=½gt3².

stem: The deceleration experienced by a moving motor boat after its engine is cut off is given by dv/dt = -k v³, where k is a positive constant. If v₀ is the speed when the engine is cut off, the speed v after traversing a distance s is:
raw_stem: The deceleration experienced by a moving motor boat after its engine is cut off is given by dv/dt = -k v³, where k is a positive constant. If v₀ is the speed when the engine is cut off, the speed v after traversing a distance s is:
subject: Physics
formula: a = v (dv/ds) = -k v³ ⇒ dv/ds = -k v²
steps: Given dv/dt = -k v³.
Transform time derivative to spatial derivative: dv/dt = v (dv/ds).
Equate: v (dv/ds) = -k v³ ⇒ dv/ds = -k v².
Separate variables: v⁻² dv = -k ds.
Integrate from s = 0 (v = v₀) to s (v = v): [-1/v]_{v₀}^v = -k s ⇒ 1/v - 1/v₀ = k s.
1/v = (1 + k s v₀) / v₀ ⇒ v = v₀ / (1 + k s v₀).
trap: dv/dt = -k v³ does NOT mean dv/ds = -k v³! Always apply the spatial chain rule a = v(dv/ds).
teacher_check: Apply dv/dt=v dv/ds, then integrate dv/ds=-kv² to obtain 1/v-1/v0=ks.

stem: A particle moves in a resistive medium with acceleration a = -β v, where β is a constant and v is instantaneous velocity. If the initial velocity is v₀ at x = 0, the maximum distance the particle can penetrate before coming to rest is:
raw_stem: A particle moves in a resistive medium with acceleration a = -β v, where β is a constant and v is instantaneous velocity. If the initial velocity is v₀ at x = 0, the maximum distance the particle can penetrate before coming to rest is:
subject: Physics
formula: a = v (dv/dx) = -β v ⇒ dv/dx = -β ⇒ Δv = -β x_max
steps: Express acceleration spatially: a = v (dv/dx).
Given a = -β v ⇒ v (dv/dx) = -β v ⇒ dv/dx = -β.
Integrate from x = 0 (v = v₀) to x_max (v = 0):
∫_{v₀}^0 dv = -β ∫₀^{x_max} dx ⇒ (0 - v₀) = -β x_max ⇒ x_max = v₀ / β.
trap: Even though it takes infinite time for velocity to asymptotically reach zero (v(t) = v₀ e^{-β t}), the total spatial penetration is strictly FINITE: x_max = v₀ / β!
teacher_check: Use v dv/dx=-βv, cancel v away from the limiting endpoint, and integrate dv/dx=-β to get xmax=v0/β.

stem: Two cars A and B travel in the same direction along a straight highway. Car A moves at constant speed v_A = 20 m/s. Car B is initially 100 m ahead of Car A and moves at constant speed v_B = 10 m/s. At t = 0, Car B begins to brake with constant deceleration a_B = 1 m/s². Find the time when Car A overtakes Car B.
raw_stem: Two cars A and B travel in the same direction along a straight highway. Car A moves at constant speed v_A = 20 m/s. Car B is initially 100 m ahead of Car A and moves at constant speed v_B = 10 m/s. At t = 0, Car B begins to brake with constant deceleration a_B = 1 m/s². Find the time when Car A overtakes Car B.
subject: Physics
formula: x_{B/A}(t) = x_{B/A}(0) + v_{rel} t + ½ a_{rel} t² = 0
steps: Set up relative coordinate frame with Car A as reference origin:
Initial relative position: x_{rel}(0) = x_B(0) - x_A(0) = +100 m.
Initial relative velocity: v_{rel} = v_B - v_A = 10 - 20 = -10 m/s.
Relative acceleration: a_{rel} = a_B - a_A = (-1) - 0 = -1 m/s².
Relative position equation: x_{rel}(t) = 100 - 10 t - 0.5 t² = 0.
Check if B stopped: t_stop = 10 / 1 = 10 s > 7.32 s. Overtaking occurs while B is still moving!
trap: Always verify whether the braking vehicle stops before overtaking happens; here 7.32 s < 10 s, so the motion is valid throughout.
teacher_check: Solve 100-10t-½t²=0 and independently check t=7.32 s is before B's 10 s stopping time.

stem: Two trains A and B, each of length 150 m, are moving in opposite directions on parallel tracks with speeds 72 km/h and 36 km/h respectively. The time of complete crossing is:
raw_stem: Two trains A and B, each of length 150 m, are moving in opposite directions on parallel tracks with speeds 72 km/h and 36 km/h respectively. The time of complete crossing is:
subject: Physics
formula: t_cross = (L_A + L_B) / v_{rel}
steps: Convert speeds to SI units: v_A = 72 × (5/18) = 20 m/s, v_B = 36 × (5/18) = 10 m/s.
Opposite directions add relative speed: v_{rel} = v_A + v_B = 20 + 10 = 30 m/s.
Total distance to clear: D = L_A + L_B = 150 + 150 = 300 m.
Crossing time: t = D / v_{rel} = 300 / 30 = 10 s.
trap: Opposite directions ADD relative velocities (20 + 10 = 30 m/s), rather than subtracting them!
teacher_check: Convert to SI, add speeds for opposite directions, and divide the sum of train lengths by relative speed.

stem: Two trains travelling on the same track are approaching each other with speeds of 40 m/s and 20 m/s respectively. When they are 1.2 km apart, both drivers simultaneously apply brakes which produce equal decelerations of 1 m/s² in each train. The collision:
raw_stem: Two trains travelling on the same track are approaching each other with speeds of 40 m/s and 20 m/s respectively. When they are 1.2 km apart, both drivers simultaneously apply brakes which produce equal decelerations of 1 m/s² in each train. The collision:
subject: Physics
formula: s₁ = u₁² / (2a₁),  s₂ = u₂² / (2a₂);  s_total = s₁ + s₂ < D_initial
steps: Calculate stopping distance of Train 1: s₁ = u₁² / (2a) = 40² / (2 × 1) = 1600 / 2 = 800 m.
Calculate stopping distance of Train 2: s₂ = u₂² / (2a) = 20² / (2 × 1) = 400 / 2 = 200 m.
Total stopping distance: s_total = s₁ + s₂ = 800 + 200 = 1000 m = 1.0 km.
Initial separation: D = 1.2 km = 1200 m.
Since s_total (1000 m) < D (1200 m), the collision is completely averted!
Remaining gap between stopped trains: Gap = 1200 - 1000 = 200 m.
trap: Do not treat both trains as one combined deceleration if they stop at different times (Train 2 stops in 20 s, Train 1 stops in 40 s)! Calculate individual stopping distances.
teacher_check: Individual stopping distances are 800 m and 200 m; their sum is 1000 m, leaving a 200 m gap from 1200 m.

stem: A body is projected with a velocity of 12 m/s at an angle of 45° with the horizontal. Find its horizontal range. (Take g = 10 m/s²)
raw_stem: A body is projected with a velocity of 12 m/s at an angle of 45° with the horizontal. Find its horizontal range. (Take g = 10 m/s²)
subject: Physics
formula: R = (u² sin 2θ) / g
steps: Launch velocity u = 12 m/s, launch angle θ = 45°, g = 10 m/s².
Compute 2θ = 90° ⇒ sin(90°) = 1.0 (condition for maximum range).
Substitute into formula: R = (12² × 1) / 10 = 144 / 10 = 14.4 m.
trap: Resolve the launch velocity into components and check whether the formula's equal-level assumptions actually hold.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "R = (u² sin 2θ) / g" and verify that the stated data reproduce 14.4 m. No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: At what angle of projection with the horizontal will the horizontal range of a projectile be equal to its maximum height?
raw_stem: At what angle of projection with the horizontal will the horizontal range of a projectile be equal to its maximum height?
subject: Physics
formula: R tan θ = 4H  (The 4H Identity)
steps: Use the universal relation between range and apex height: R tan θ = 4H.
Apply problem condition R = H: H tan θ = 4H ⇒ tan θ = 4.
Solve for angle: θ = arctan(4) ≈ 75.96° ≈ 76°.
trap: Resolve the launch velocity into components and check whether the formula's equal-level assumptions actually hold.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "R tan θ = 4H  (The 4H Identity)" and verify that the stated data reproduce θ = arctan(4) ≈ 76°. No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: A shore defense gun fires at a pirate ship anchored at R = 560 m with muzzle speed v₀ = 82 m/s. Find: (a) The two projection angles to hit the ship, (b) The time of flight in each case. (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
raw_stem: A shore defense gun fires at a pirate ship anchored at R = 560 m with muzzle speed v₀ = 82 m/s. Find: (a) The two projection angles to hit the ship, (b) The time of flight in each case. (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
subject: Physics
formula: sin 2θ = (g R) / v₀²,  T = (2v₀ sin θ) / g
steps: First solution: 2θ₁ = arcsin(0.8162) ≈ 54.7° ⇒ θ₁ ≈ 27.4° (low flat trajectory).
Second solution: 2θ₂ = 180° - 54.7° = 125.3° ⇒ θ₂ ≈ 62.6° (high lob trajectory).
Time of flight T₁ = (2 × 82 × sin 27.4°) / 9.8 ≈ 7.69 s.
Time of flight T₂ = (2 × 82 × sin 62.6°) / 9.8 ≈ 14.86 s ≈ 15 s.
Invariant Check: T₁ × T₂ = 7.69 × 14.86 = 114.3 s² = 2R/g = 2(560)/9.8 = 114.3 s².
trap: Keep a frame label on every velocity before adding or subtracting vectors; dropping the frame is the usual sign/direction error.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "sin 2θ = (g R) / v₀²,  T = (2v₀ sin θ) / g" and verify that the stated data reproduce θ₁ ≈ 27.4°, θ₂ ≈ 62.6°; T₁ ≈ 7.7 s, T₂ ≈ 14.9 s. No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: An outfielder tracks a fly ball hit with u = 40 m/s at θ = 35°. The line-of-sight elevation angle is φ(t) with tan φ(t) = y(t) / (D - x(t)). Analyze the optical curvature d²φ/dt².
raw_stem: An outfielder tracks a fly ball hit with u = 40 m/s at θ = 35°. The line-of-sight elevation angle is φ(t) with tan φ(t) = y(t) / (D - x(t)). Analyze the optical curvature d²φ/dt².
subject: Physics
correct: tan φ is linear in t, but φ is not: d²φ/dt² = −2k³t/(1+k²t²)², where k = g/[2(u_x−v_f)].
formula: Let k = g/[2(u_x-v_f)]. On the ideal interception path, tan φ = kt, so φ = arctan(kt).
steps: For a catch-course geometry, the remaining horizontal separation is proportional to (T−t), while y(t)=½gt(T−t). The common factor (T−t) cancels.
Therefore tan φ(t)=kt with k=g/[2(u_x−v_f)]. What is linear is tan φ, not φ itself.
Differentiate φ=arctan(kt): dφ/dt=k/(1+k²t²) and d²φ/dt²=−2k³t/(1+k²t²)². For k>0 and t>0 the angular curvature is negative, not zero.
trap: The tempting cancellation proves tan φ ∝ t. It does not prove φ ∝ t or d²φ/dt²=0.
teacher_check: Differentiate arctan(kt) twice. The second derivative is nonzero for t>0 unless k=0.

stem: A stone is thrown horizontally from a cliff h = 490 m high with speed u = 98 m/s. Find: (a) time to hit ground, (b) horizontal distance from cliff base, (c) striking velocity. (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
raw_stem: A stone is thrown horizontally from a cliff h = 490 m high with speed u = 98 m/s. Find: (a) time to hit ground, (b) horizontal distance from cliff base, (c) striking velocity. (Take g = 9.8 m/s²)
subject: Physics
correct: t = 10 s, R = 980 m, v = 98√2 m/s at 45° below horizontal
formula: t = √(2h/g),  R = u t,  v = √(u² + 2gh),  tan β = gt / u
steps: Time to ground depends solely on vertical drop: t = √(2 × 490 / 9.8) = √100 = 10 s.
Horizontal distance: R = u × t = 98 × 10 = 980 m.
Velocity components at impact: v_x = 98 m/s (unchanged), v_y = gt = 9.8 × 10 = 98 m/s.
Total speed: v = √(98² + 98²) = 98√2 m/s ≈ 138.6 m/s.
Direction: tan β = v_y / v_x = 98 / 98 = 1 ⇒ β = 45° below horizontal.
trap: Do not use ground-to-ground symmetric projectile formulas when launch and landing heights differ; solve the vertical boundary event first.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "t = √(2h/g),  R = u t,  v = √(u² + 2gh),  tan β = gt / u" and verify that the stated data reproduce t = 10 s, R = 980 m, v = 98√2 m/s at 45° below horizontal. No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: Car A moves east at 1 m/s, Car B moves west at 2 m/s along a straight road. Find the relative velocity of Car B with respect to Car A.
raw_stem: Car A moves east at 1 m/s, Car B moves west at 2 m/s along a straight road. Find the relative velocity of Car B with respect to Car A.
subject: Physics
formula: v_B/A = v_B - v_A
steps: Assign coordinate direction: East = +î, West = -î.
Velocity vectors: v_A = +1 î m/s, v_B = -2 î m/s.
Relative velocity formula: v_B/A = (-2 î) - (+1 î) = -3 î m/s.
Magnitude is 3 m/s directed westward (rate of mutual approach).

teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "v_B/A = v_B - v_A" and verify that the stated data reproduce -3 î m/s (3 m/s towards West). No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: Rain falls vertically at 15 m/s. A cyclist moves horizontally at 5√3 m/s. In which direction should the cyclist hold his umbrella to protect himself?
raw_stem: Rain falls vertically at 15 m/s. A cyclist moves horizontally at 5√3 m/s. In which direction should the cyclist hold his umbrella to protect himself?
subject: Physics
formula: v_r/c = v_r - v_c,  tan θ = v_c / v_r
steps: Rain velocity: v_r = -15 ĵ m/s. Cyclist velocity: v_c = 5√3 î m/s.
Relative velocity of rain: v_r/c = v_r - v_c = -5√3 î - 15 ĵ m/s.
Tilt angle with vertical: tan θ = |v_cx| / |v_ry| = (5√3) / 15 = 1/√3.
Solve for angle: θ = arctan(1/√3) = 30° forward.
trap: Keep a frame label on every velocity before adding or subtracting vectors; dropping the frame is the usual sign/direction error.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "v_r/c = v_r - v_c,  tan θ = v_c / v_r" and verify that the stated data reproduce 30° forward with the vertical. No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: A car travels East at 80 km/h. To a passenger in the car, a train appears to move due North at 80√3 km/h. Find the actual velocity of the train.
raw_stem: A car travels East at 80 km/h. To a passenger in the car, a train appears to move due North at 80√3 km/h. Find the actual velocity of the train.
subject: Physics
formula: v_train = v_train/car + v_car
steps: Car velocity: v_car = 80 î km/h. Apparent train velocity: v_t/c = 80√3 ĵ km/h.
Reconstruct true train velocity: v_t = v_t/c + v_car = 80 î + 80√3 ĵ km/h.
Direction: tan θ = (80√3) / 80 = √3 ⇒ θ = 60° North of East.
trap: Keep a frame label on every velocity before adding or subtracting vectors; dropping the frame is the usual sign/direction error.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "v_train = v_train/car + v_car" and verify that the stated data reproduce 160 km/h at 60° North of East. No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: An airplane wishes to fly towards 45° North of East. Wind blows from West at 40 km/h. Airspeed is 200 km/h. Find steering heading using the Sine Rule.
raw_stem: An airplane wishes to fly towards 45° North of East. Wind blows from West at 40 km/h. Airspeed is 200 km/h. Find steering heading using the Sine Rule.
subject: Physics
correct: Steer 53.13° North of East, i.e. 8.13° north of the desired 45° track to compensate for the eastward wind.
formula: v_ground = v_air + v_wind; desired track requires v_gy = v_gx.
steps: Wind 'from West' points East: v_wind = 40 î km/h.
Let the aircraft heading be ψ North of East. Then v_ground=(200 cosψ+40)î+200 sinψ ĵ.
For a 45° ground track, set 200 sinψ = 200 cosψ + 40, so sinψ−cosψ=0.2.
Thus √2 sin(ψ−45°)=0.2, giving ψ−45°≈8.13° and ψ≈53.13° North of East.
trap: Subtracting the 8.13° correction steers with the eastward wind; the correction must be toward the upwind side of the desired track.
teacher_check: Resolve the corrected heading: 200 sin53.13° and 200 cos53.13°+40 are equal, so the ground track is exactly 45°.

stem: A river flows East at 2 m/s. A boat motors upstream (West) at 5 m/s in water. A person walks towards the stern (East) at 3 m/s on the boat. Find person's velocity w.r.t ground.
raw_stem: A river flows East at 2 m/s. A boat motors upstream (West) at 5 m/s in water. A person walks towards the stern (East) at 3 m/s on the boat. Find person's velocity w.r.t ground.
subject: Physics
formula: v_p/g = v_p/b + v_b/w + v_w/g  (Three-Body Chaining)
steps: Define East as +î. River flow w.r.t ground: v_w/g = +2 î m/s.
Boat w.r.t water: v_b/w = -5 î m/s (upstream).
Person w.r.t boat: v_p/b = +3 î m/s (towards stern, i.e., East).
Chain reference frames: v_p/g = (+3 î) + (-5 î) + (+2 î) = (3 - 5 + 2) î = 0 î m/s.
trap: Keep a frame label on every velocity before adding or subtracting vectors; dropping the frame is the usual sign/direction error.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "v_p/g = v_p/b + v_b/w + v_w/g  (Three-Body Chaining)" and verify that the stated data reproduce 0 m/s (Stationary w.r.t riverbank!). No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: A man walking at 3 km/h observes rain falling vertically. At 6 km/h, rain appears at 45° to vertical. Find the actual velocity of the rain.
raw_stem: A man walking at 3 km/h observes rain falling vertically. At 6 km/h, rain appears at 45° to vertical. Find the actual velocity of the rain.
subject: Physics
correct: 3√2 km/h at 45° with vertical (falling towards East)
formula: v_r = v_rx î - v_ry ĵ,  v_r/m = (v_rx - v_m) î - v_ry ĵ
steps: At v_m1 = 3 î km/h: rain appears vertical ⇒ apparent horizontal component is zero ⇒ v_rx - 3 = 0 ⇒ v_rx = 3 km/h.
At v_m2 = 6 î km/h: relative horizontal velocity is 6 - 3 = 3 km/h backward.
Given apparent angle is 45° with vertical: tan 45° = |v_rx - 6| / v_ry = 3 / v_ry = 1 ⇒ v_ry = 3 km/h.
True rain velocity: v_r = 3 î - 3 ĵ km/h.
Magnitude: |v_r| = √(3² + 3²) = 3√2 km/h ≈ 4.24 km/h.
Direction: tan θ = 3 / 3 = 1 ⇒ θ = 45° with vertical (falling forward at 45°).
trap: Keep a frame label on every velocity before adding or subtracting vectors; dropping the frame is the usual sign/direction error.
teacher_check: Independent check: re-derive from "v_r = v_rx î - v_ry ĵ,  v_r/m = (v_rx - v_m) î - v_ry ĵ" and verify that the stated data reproduce 3√2 km/h at 45° with vertical (falling towards East). No unstated numerical parameter should be needed.

stem: Two identical bodies, projected with the same speed at two different angles cover the same horizontal range R . If the time of flight of these bodies are 5 s and 10 s , respectively, then the value of R is ____ m. (Take g=10m/s2 )

formula: t₁ + t₂ = T = (2u sin θ) / g
